title: Recursively split crowded price buckets
summary: Start with three broad price buckets. Recursively split the crowded buckets containing 65% and 35% of the data to get seven more evenly sized leaf buckets.
context: Each percentage is a share of all products, not a share of that bucket’s parent. The figure supplies price-range labels and percentages but gives no total product count, currency unit, or complete convention for interval endpoints.
description: Arrows from “Product data” show successive subdivisions. Buckets with no further splits remain leaves. The first level has three price buckets: <100 holds 65%, 100–500 holds 20%, and >500 holds 15%. Because the <100 bucket holds 65% of all products, split it into three child buckets.

At the second level, <100 splits into <10 with 18%, 10–50 with 35%, and 50–100 with 12%. Their shares sum to 18% + 35% + 12% = 65%. The 10–50 bucket still holds a high share (35%), so split it again into 10–20 with 13%, 20–35 with 12%, and 35–50 with 10%. Their sum is 13% + 12% + 10% = 35%.

“Data partitioning result” on the right lists the seven leaf buckets (see the table). Each holds between 10% and 20% of the data, more even than the initial 65%, 20%, and 15%. The intermediate 65% and 35% represent split parents and do not count again among the final buckets.

frames.title: Recursively split crowded price buckets
frames.explanation: The seven leaf percentages add to 100%. Each holds 10% to 20%, so the counts are more evenly distributed. An implementation must complete the illustrated ranges by specifying how to assign their endpoints.
